I'm still going over the science of strength training and forcing it to apply to calisthenics, so the routine might change substantially by the time I'm willing to post it to /v/bodyweightfitness. I'm not sure how well self-directed beginners can learn to do max-effort exercises, but I have repeated warnings all over the whole thing. Isometrics especially, they'll make you crazy sore.

Any and all criticism, either about the routine itself, the wisdom of calling it a beginner routine, or about the choppy writing is welcome. I'll release the remainder of the routine when it's done and I've run through it a few times.

-----

The skill work in this routine, and in most calisthenics routines is practicing the free-standing handstand. I suggest 5-10 minutes daily. There's a lot of perfectly good guides to learning handstands out there, and this isn't one of them. Just practice kicking up into a handstand, holding the frog and crow stand positions, and just get used to being upside down. Since the handstand progression in this routine is meant to be done against a wall, the skill work isn't totally necessary anyway.

Isometric training is a style of training in which the muscles tense up, but don't move. All maximal strength efforts are done at a "quasi-isometric" speed, since no one lifts their 1 rep max quickly. The benefits of isometric training is that they allow for maximal effort, and therefore maximal strength gains, for very little time or energy expenditure. The main disadvantages are: lack of carryover to speed and power based exercises, the exercise builds neuromuscular strength but not biomechanical strength, and the gains are limited in range of motion, with almost complete strength carryover over 15 degrees of the joint angle, and smaller benefits over the full range. Typically the range of strength increase is greater when isometrics are trained with elongated muscles. They are perfectly safe, but they will make you incredibly sore if overdone. Even for Olympic athletes, doing these for more than 10 minutes is a terrible idea.

It's not as simple as tensing up though, every isometric contraction involves a *rise time* as it contracts from a relaxed state, a *resistance phase* as it sustains this contraction, and a *decay time* as it returns to rest or a lower value. Isometrics can be used for holding gymnastic poses, build explosive power, or to improve performance in dynamic exercises. When training for strength you apply force gradually (2-4s) contract as hard as you can (100% effort) for 6-8s, no longer. Rest 5-10s between repetitions, and repeat up to 6 times for a given position. For training explosive power (rate of tension production, actually) you try to get to 70-80% maximal effort as quickly as possible.

L-sits, bridges, and planks are the isometric holds we'll be training. You may wish to add wall sits, and holds based various dynamic movements you're having trouble progressing in. The bottom of the pistol squat is a common one. One of the biggest factors in isometric training is muscle temperature, so they might be easier before warming up, or after exposure to cold temperatures. Just a thought.

The L-sit (half-lever to gymnasts) is one of the hardest bodyweight exercises for beginners, and it tends to progress more slowly than other skills. You may substitute hanging leg raises in the progression. The easiest progression is the "tuck L-sit" or "N-sit" Try it from the floor, if you still can't get your shoulders down enough do it from parallel bars. Push down through your scapula, tuck your knees to your chest, and keep your butt of the floor. Hold for 6 seconds. Rest 5-10s repeat for 3-5 sets.

The bridge is good for lower back health, you may consider just doing these for time. We start with the short bridge, which consists of lying on your back and lifting your butt in the air with your legs, and pull your torso towards your feet. You should feel this one in your glutes. Advance by putting your hands next to your head and lifting the rest of yourself in the air for the *full bridge* and from there you can lift an arm or leg off the ground for increased variation. Hold for 6 seconds. Rest 5-10s repeat for 3-5 sets.

The other isometric exercise is the plank. You can probably hold this one a lot longer than 6-8s, so we'll make it harder. Do it with your feet on the wall for a wall plank. Bring your hands down below your shoulders for the planche lean. From there, work on your tuck planche. Keep going until you find something you can hold for 6 seconds. You get the idea.

So the beginner's isometric routine will look like: ~~~ L-sit progression 6s hold, 3-5 reps. Bridge progression 6s, 3-5 reps. Plank progressions 6s, 3-5 reps. ~~~ So this will take 2-5 minutes.

The goal is to maintain as close to 100 percent tension as you possibly can, but you may simply do these exercises for time, if that's what you want. Easier to quantify too.

Shock Training

Pliometrics (also known as jump stuff, plyometrics, and shock training) is not recommended for beginners or people with tendon or joint problems. In fact, they're mostly designed for and tested by high-level athletes. That's not to say that the training method is ineffective for beginner-intermediate athletes, it's simply riskier and less effective. I advise caution, and 6-8 weeks experience with the isometric portion of the routine before doing these.

We'll be utilizing the stretch reflex to increase power output on two exercises, the depth jump and the explosive push-up. The stretch reflex will be activated by a controlled jump off a platform for the squat jump, and the explosive push-up you'll have to drop into, preferably from a kneeling position. The stretch should be rapid, no more than 1.2-1.5 seconds, the stretch should be deep, enough to trigger the myotatic response and the contraction on your end should be initiated at the same time as you hit the ground. There's no need to clap or tuck your legs in mid-air, but you can consider those as progressions. You'll want to increase the drop height as your muscles get better at storing elastic energy, and as your tendons adapt to the strain. Sets of 10 seem to be the most optimal for this style of training. Repeat the exercises from the starting position.

For the depth jump: jump off something, the exact height isn't important, don't squat down anywhere near parallel, a slight hip angle is good, and jump as your feet touch the ground.

For the explosive push-up: get two raised platforms on either side of you (the same set-up you would use for an increased range of motion push-up.) Fall into them, catching yourself in a push-up position, push yourself up as your hands hit the platforms. Repeat the process from the top. Clap if you want to. Rest as long as you need to between sets.

~~~ Depth jumps 2 x 10 Explosive Push-ups 2 x 10 ~~~
